question: In her State of the Union Address, the President of the Commission stated that ‘the events of this summer show that our tools need to evolve – especially for emergency situations. Europe needs the means to protect its borders at all times. Especially in scenarios when mass movements are engineered and weaponised. This is why we will propose a new European Emergency Response Framework’.

1 Commissioner Magnus Brunner is also reportedly considering the possibility of suspending the granting of asylum at the EU’s external border in situations similar to the crisis in Ceuta. We have repeatedly called for the introduction of such measures in letters, parliamentary questions addressed to the Commission, amendments to legislative acts and during exchanges of views with its representatives.
However, the Commission has stubbornly persisted with its misguided ideological policy, the disastrous effects of which we have seen yet again in Ceuta. 1.

In the Commission’s view, how does the situation in Ceuta differ from the situation at the border with Belarus since 2021? Why did the Commission fail to support the Polish authorities at that time, leaving the protection of the EU’s external border to the determination, commitment and steadfastness of the Polish authorities and security services?

Why did the Commission withdraw Regulation 2021/0427(COD) addressing situations of instrumentalisation in the field of migration and asylum2, and does the Commission, having analysed its errors, agree that in the event of hybrid attacks on the EU’s external borders – as has been the case since 2021 on the border with Belarus or, more recently, in Ceuta, Spain – it is justified to temporarily suspend asylum procedures at the border and turn back migrants who are residing lawfully on the territory of a country neighbouring the EU?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.11.2026) The Commission stands firmly with Member States facing weaponisation and instrumentalisation of migration. The EU has taken several steps since 2021 to counter the instrumentalisation of migrants by Belarus and Russia. Financial, operational and diplomatic efforts, including with the countries of origin and transit, were promptly stepped up.

In December 2024, the Commission made available additional EUR 170 million under the Border Management and Visa Instrument to strengthen surveillance at the borders with Russia and Belarus, including EUR 52 million for Poland.

Furthermore, in its 2024 Communication on countering hybrid threats from the weaponisation of migration and strengthening security at the EU’s external borders1, the Commission stepped up its support to Member States facing those threats, setting the framework for actions that should prevent Russia and Belarus from using the EU's principles and values against the EU.

The Commission withdrew proposal COM (2021)890 because its substance had been incorporated into Regulation (EU) 2024/1359 addressing situations of crisis and force majeure in the field of migration and asylum and amending Regulation (EU) 2021/11472.
1 Communication from the Commission to the European Parliament and the Council on countering hybrid threats

from the weaponisation of migration and strengthening security at the EU’s external borders, COM (2024) 570 final, Brussels, 11 December 2024. 2 Regulation (EU) 2024/1359 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 May 2024 addressing situations of crisis and force majeure in the field of migration and asylum and amending Regulation (EU) 2021/1147; OJ L, 2024/1359, 22.5.2024.
